content: 1. The development of cirrhosis and initiation of antiviral therapy are critical to prevent progression to hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) or liver failure. 2. Following a reactive HCV antibody serological test result, it is recommended to use either quantitative or qualitative nucleic acid testing (NAT) to detect HCV RNA as the preferred method for diagnosing viremic infection. This recommendation is based on strong evidence, albeit of moderate to low quality. 3. An alternative to NAT for diagnosing viremic HCV infection is the use of an assay to detect HCV core antigen (p22), which has comparable clinical sensitivity to NAT. This assay can be used at the point of care or with dried blood spot specimens and is more affordable. An assay with a detection limit of 3000 IU/mL or lower is acceptable and can identify 95% of viremic infections based on available data. 4. Approximately 15–45% of individuals infected with HCV will spontaneously clear the infection. These individuals remain HCV antibody-positive but are no longer infected with HCV. Diagnosing viremic HCV infection in antibody-positive individuals helps distinguish those who need treatment from those who have cleared the infection. 5. NAT technologies, both quantitative and qualitative, are widely used for detecting viremic HCV infection. Quantitative NAT is commonly employed to measure viral load, identify those requiring treatment, and assess treatment response. Qualitative NAT provides rapid and sensitive detection of the virus and evidence of a decline in viral RNA levels below a defined threshold. 6. There are currently five commercially available quantitative HCV RNA assays, with two more in development. While NAT technologies are highly sensitive and specific for detecting viremia, they require sophisticated laboratory equipment and skilled personnel. Recently, point-of-care NAT assays for HCV RNA detection have become commercially available, improving accessibility. 7. HCV core antigen (HCVcAg) testing is another method for detecting viremic HCV infection. HCVcAg, a nucleocapsid peptide (p22), is released into plasma during viral assembly and can be detected early in the course of infection. Serological methods for HCVcAg detection are potentially less costly and more centralized than NAT, but their evaluation in low-resource settings has been limited. 8. Several standalone HCVcAg assays are now commercially available. HCVcAg detection has also been incorporated into fourth-generation HCV Ag/Ab serological assays to increase sensitivity in early infection. However, these assays are not intended to differentiate seropositivity from active viremic infection. 9. NAT assays are considered the reference standard for detecting viremia, but studies comparing quantitative and qualitative NAT assays for viremia detection are limited in number and quality. The overall evidence for using HCVcAg as an alternative to NAT is rated as low to moderate due to inconsistency and imprecision. 10. The Guidelines Development Group strongly recommends using NAT assays (quantitative or qualitative) as the preferred strategy for diagnosing viremic HCV infection. This recommendation is based on moderateto low-quality evidence and the high sensitivity of NAT assays, which can detect viral loads as low as 15 IU/mL. 11. HCVcAg assays are recognized as a potentially lower-cost alternative to NAT for diagnosing viremic HCV infection. These assays can utilize existing serological testing platforms and may serve as a more affordable replacement for NAT in the future. However, there is significant variability in sensitivity and specificity among different HCVcAg assays. 12. HCVcAg tests may also be used as a one-step screening test in high-prevalence settings, as HCVcAg appears earlier than HCV antibodies. However, this strategy is cost-effective only in very high-prevalence settings, and there is a risk of missing cases due to reduced clinical sensitivity. 13. The Guidelines Development Group recommends using NAT detection of HCV RNA as a test of cure at 12 weeks (or 24 weeks if 12 weeks is not possible) after completing treatment. Qualitative NAT assays are preferred due to their lower cost compared to quantitative NAT assays. 14. HCVcAg testing has been proposed as an alternative to NAT for diagnosing viremic HCV infection and assessing treatment response. However, there is ongoing debate about its utility as a tool for monitoring treatment response and testing for cure. 15. The high cost and limited availability of NAT testing for HCV RNA present barriers to widespread implementation in resource-limited settings. HCVcAg assays, while less expensive, still face challenges in terms of sensitivity, specificity, and availability. 16. The use of point-of-care or near-patient technologies for HCV diagnosis offers the potential for same-day diagnosis of viremic infection, improving access to care and reducing loss to follow-up. These devices are more affordable than laboratory-based NAT assays and can facilitate early diagnosis, monitoring, and linkage to treatment services. 17. Immediate NAT testing following a positive serological result is valuable for distinguishing resolved HCV infections from viremic infections, allowing for prompt referral for care and treatment. 18. Genotyping remains important for determining the most appropriate treatment regimen, as HCV genotypes vary among individuals with chronic HCV infection. However, genotyping is expensive and not universally available. As pangenotypic regimens become more accessible, the need for genotyping may diminish. 19. The cost of quantitative NAT testing ranges from $30 to $200 per test, while HCVcAg testing costs $25–50. Both options remain financially burdensome, particularly in resource-limited settings. 20. The Guidelines Development Group emphasizes the need for further evaluation of the diagnostic accuracy, cost-effectiveness, and impact of HCVcAg and HCV RNA assays as one-step diagnostic strategies.
